notes.b: Whatever the implement (the object being thrown), the aim is the same: make it travel as far as possible. Three factors decide how far it goes, and one body mechanism produces the speed.
points: Distance depends mainly on release speed (how fast the implement is moving as it leaves the hand), then on release angle (the angle it leaves at) and release height.

Summation of forces, also called the kinetic chain, means force is generated from the legs, passes through the hips and trunk, then to the shoulder, arm and hand in sequence, with each segment adding speed to the one before.
A long, straight throwing arm at release lengthens the lever (the arm acts as a rigid bar turning about the shoulder), which increases the speed of release.
notes.tip: Exams use throws as contexts for the javelin as a third-class lever, so link a long, straight arm to a longer lever and greater release speed.

notes.h: Rules common to the circle throws
notes.b: Shot-put, discus and hammer are thrown from a marked circle into a sector (the marked landing area). The same rules apply to all three, and breaking them makes the throw a foul (an illegal throw that does not count).
points: The throw starts from a stationary position inside the circle, so the thrower cannot begin moving before entering it.
The implement must land within the sector, otherwise the throw does not count.
The thrower must not touch the top of the stop board (the raised curved board at the front of the shot-put circle) or step on or outside the circle's edge.
The thrower leaves the circle from the back half, and only after the implement has landed.
A thrower who leaves the circle before the implement lands commits a foul.

notes.b: The shot is put (pushed) rather than thrown. The technique builds speed from the legs and hips and finishes with a push from the neck.
points: Grip: the shot rests on the fingers at their base, not in the palm, and is tucked into the neck under the jaw.
Stance and preparation: the athlete stands at the back of the circle facing away from the throwing direction, with the elbow held high.

Movement into the throw: the athlete moves across the circle by a glide (a low travelling movement backwards across the circle) or a rotational movement (a spin), drives from the legs, and turns the hips.
Release: the shot is pushed from the neck at about 40 degrees, the typical optimum release angle, with a wrist flick that adds final speed.
Follow-through: a reverse (switching the feet after release) stops the athlete's momentum carrying them out, so they stay in the circle.
Key rules: the shot is pushed, not thrown; a throwing action from behind the shoulder is a foul.
Safety: no cage (the protective netting around the circle) is used for the shot, so the sector must be checked clear before each put.
notes.tip: The shot is pushed, not thrown, and a throwing action from behind the shoulder is a foul. Say 'about 40 degrees' for the release angle. Exams also ask for a component of fitness for shot-put.

notes.b: The discus is a flat disc thrown after spinning across the circle. The turn builds speed and the spin on release keeps the discus stable in flight.
points: Grip: the fingertips are spread over the rim of the discus, with the palm facing down.
Stance and preparation: the athlete stands at the back of the circle, so there is room to turn, and makes preliminary swings (practice swings of the arm) to build the turn.
Movement into the throw: the athlete makes a turn of one and a half rotations across the circle, with the arm long and straight, sweeping round at shoulder height.

The turn happens in the transverse plane (a horizontal plane that divides the body into top and bottom halves) about the longitudinal axis (an imaginary line running from head to toe). There is more on this in Analysing skill: the biomechanical perspective.
Release and follow-through: the discus is released off the index finger, spinning clockwise for a right-hander, and a reverse (switching the feet) keeps the athlete in the circle.
Key rules: the discus is thrown with its spin set up in the turn, and its flight is judged by where it lands in the sector.
Safety: discus is thrown from a cage, so the cage must be in place before the turns begin.
notes.tip: Discus and hammer rotation is in the transverse plane about the longitudinal axis. Exams ask for the plane and axis of these turns, so name both.

notes.b: The javelin is a long spear thrown after a run-up rather than a spin. The thrower builds speed on the approach, then transfers it through a braced front leg.
points: Grip: held behind the cord (the binding on the shaft), using a grip such as the Finnish or American grip.
Stance and preparation: the javelin is carried above the shoulder during the approach run (the run-up before the throw).

Movement into the throw: over the last strides the javelin is withdrawn back with a straight arm, followed by cross-over (impulse) steps, where the legs cross to keep the hips ahead of the javelin, then the front leg is planted.
Release: the hips and then the shoulders rotate, and the elbow leads over the shoulder, passing force up the kinetic chain in order.
Follow-through: the throw is made over a braced front leg (a firm, straight leg that blocks forward movement) at about 30-35 degrees along the line of the shaft, the typical optimum release angle.
Key rules: the javelin must land tip first in the sector.
Safety: the approach run passes ahead of the thrower, so the javelin is not thrown until the area in front is clear.
notes.tip: The javelin must land tip first. Say 'about 30-35 degrees' for the release angle. Exams ask for the javelin as a third-class lever and for practice methods for a javelin thrower.

notes.b: The hammer is swung round the head and turned with the body to build speed, and it is thrown from a cage for protection.
points: Grip: both hands hold the handle of the hammer.
Stance and preparation: preliminary winds (swings) of the hammer are made around the head, to get it moving before the turns begin.
Movement into the throw: three or four accelerating turns are made on the heels and toes, with long straight arms, which keeps the hammer in a wide orbit so it gains speed.
These turns happen in the transverse plane (a horizontal plane dividing the body into top and bottom halves) about the longitudinal axis (a line running from head to toe).
Release and follow-through: the hammer passes through a low point and a high point of its orbit (the circular path it travels), and is released over the left shoulder for a right-hander.
Key rules: the hammer is thrown from a cage, which must be fully in place before the throw.
Safety: the cage contains the turns and the release, so the thrower stays inside it until the hammer has left the hand.
notes.tip: Discus and hammer rotation is in the transverse plane about the longitudinal axis. Exams ask for the plane and axis of these turns, so name both.

notes.b: Efficient throwing means the whole body works as one chain, which is why a single weak link wastes speed. Knowing what efficient technique looks like also tells you what the faults are.
points: Efficient throwing is a smooth rhythm, with balance in the circle and the kinetic chain sequenced from the legs to the hand.
A blocked or braced front side lets the force from the legs transfer into the throw, rather than the body carrying on forward.
Fault: throwing with the arm only, without a leg drive, loses most of the available speed because the strongest muscles are not used.
Fault: opening the shoulders too early ends the rotation before release.
Fault: a low release angle sends the implement flat and short.
Fault: falling out of the circle during the throw is a foul.
notes.tip: For efficiency, name the smooth rhythm, balance in the circle, the sequenced kinetic chain and the blocked or braced front side. Exams also ask about training with light and heavy implements.

notes.b: Throwing implements are heavy and can travel a long way, so strict habits protect everyone on the field.
points: Throw only on command, and retrieve only on command, so nobody walks into the sector while a throw is being made.
Carry implements back to the thrower; never throw them back, because a thrown implement can hit someone.
Stay behind the thrower while a throw is being made, so you are never in the line of the throw.
Check the sector is clear before each throw, so no one is struck by the implement.

keyTerms.definition: The sequential transfer of force from the legs through the hips, trunk, shoulder and arm to the implement, with each segment adding speed.
The linked sequence of body segments that transfers force from the ground up to the implement in a throw.
The marked area into which a throw must land to count.
The board at the front of the circle that the thrower must not touch.
A movement across the shot-put circle in which the thrower moves backwards and across, staying low.
A movement in which the thrower switches feet to turn back and stay inside the circle after a throw.
The impulse steps of the javelin approach, in which the feet cross to build speed before the front leg is planted.
The backward movement of the javelin over the last strides, with a straight arm, before the throw.
The swings used at the start of a discus or hammer throw to build momentum before the turns.
The horizontal plane in which discus and hammer turns occur, about the longitudinal axis.

factCards.term: Factors that determine distance in throwing
factCards.definition: Release speed first, then release angle, then release height.

factCards.term: Shot-put: the sequence of the throw
factCards.definition: Grip at the base of the fingers and shot tucked in the neck; stance at the back of the circle; glide or rotation; drive from the legs and hip turn; push from the neck at about 40 degrees; reverse to stay in the circle.

factCards.term: Discus: the sequence of the throw
factCards.definition: Fingertips over the rim; preliminary swings; turn of one and a half rotations; long straight arm sweeping at shoulder height; release off the index finger; reverse to stay in the circle.

factCards.term: Javelin: the sequence of the throw
factCards.definition: Grip behind the cord; approach carried above the shoulder; withdrawal with a straight arm; cross-over steps; plant front leg; hips then shoulders rotate; release at about 30-35 degrees.

factCards.term: Hammer: the sequence of the throw
factCards.definition: Two-handed grip; preliminary winds; three or four accelerating turns; low and high points of the orbit; release over the left shoulder for a right-hander; thrown from a cage.

questions.prompt: Describe the grip, movement into the throw and release of one throwing event, and explain how the summation of forces increases release speed.
questions.model: Shot-put: the shot rests on the fingers at their base and is tucked into the neck under the jaw, with the elbow held high. The thrower stands at the back of the circle, moves across it by a glide or rotation, and drives from the legs with a hip turn. The shot is pushed from the neck at about 40 degrees with a wrist flick, and the thrower reverses feet to stay in the circle. Summation of forces: force generated from the legs passes through the hips and trunk to the shoulder, arm and hand in sequence, and each segment adds speed as it passes on the force. A braced front side stops the force being lost, and a long, straight throwing arm at release lengthens the lever, so the shot leaves the hand faster.

questions.prompt: Outline three safety rules that apply in throwing events.
questions.model: First, athletes throw only on command and retrieve implements only on command, so nobody is in the sector when a throw is made. Second, implements are carried back to the thrower rather than thrown back, so nobody is struck returning them. Third, the sector is checked clear before each throw and nobody walks across it while throws are being made; discus and hammer are also thrown from cages, which must be in place before the throw.
